The piddock Barnea parva is a wood-boring bivalve typical of intertidal and shallow subtidal habitats along European coasts. Field surveys of reproductively active individuals indicate that the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches an average of 12% [GSI = 12%] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This value was derived from dissections of several dozen adults collected during the peak spawning season, with each individual's gonad mass expressed relative to its total soft-tissue mass. The index is notably lower than values reported for some co-occurring pholadids, possibly because Barnea parva inhabits physically stressful, frequently disturbed soft-rock substrata that constrain the scope for energetic investment in gamete production.

The maximum shell length attained by Barnea parva rarely exceeds 4.6 centimeters [Li = 4.6 centimeters] in well-sampled populations, a size that appears to represent an asymptotic limit under typical environmental conditions. This ultimate total length was estimated from longitudinal growth studies of marked individuals in a sheltered sea-lough population followed over several years. Growth trajectories in this species are strongly decelerating, with most of the length increase occurring within the first 12 to 18 months after larval settlement, after which shell accretion slows markedly. The relatively modest adult size compared with other members of the Pholadidae may reflect constraints imposed by the limited dimensions of available burrows in soft chalk or clay substrata, as well as the energetic costs of maintaining a functional siphon in a burrowing lifestyle.

Sexual maturation in Barnea parva is tightly linked to body size rather than age, with individuals becoming capable of reproduction upon reaching a total shell length of 1.7 centimeters [Lp = 1.7 centimeters]. This length at puberty was determined through histological examination of gonadal tissue in a size-graded series of specimens collected monthly over two consecutive reproductive seasons, revealing that the onset of gametogenesis coincides consistently with the attainment of that critical shell dimension. The relationship between size and maturation is ecologically meaningful, as it ensures that only animals with sufficient burrow volume and filtering capacity invest in reproduction, thereby avoiding futile spawning attempts by individuals too small to accommodate developing gonads. This size threshold is relatively small when compared to the ultimate length of 4.6 centimeters [Li = 4.6 centimeters], meaning that Barnea parva attains reproductive competence at roughly 37 percent of its asymptotic size, a value near the middle of the range reported for other infaunal bivalves.

Somatic mass at the onset of reproduction has been quantified from dry-weight measurements of individuals collected at the size threshold for puberty. The dry weight at puberty is 0.0353 grams , a value derived from desiccated soft tissues of specimens measuring precisely 1.7 centimeters in shell length, after removal of all shell material and careful blotting to remove adherent water. Correspondingly, the ultimate dry weight—the maximum somatic mass approached by fully grown adults—reaches 0.634 grams , representing a roughly eighteen-fold increase in dry tissue mass between the onset of reproductive maturity and the asymptotic body size. This substantial post-puberty growth increment underscores the importance of continued somatic investment after first maturation, a pattern common among long-lived iteroparous bivalves that accrue reproductive output gradually over successive spawning seasons while still adding somatic tissue.

The reproductive process begins with the release of minute eggs, the wet weight at birth of a newly spawned ovum being approximately 0.00000097 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00000097 grams], a value calculated from the measured egg diameter of 123 micrometers using the standard spherical volume formula. Following external fertilisation, the resulting veliger larvae embark on a planktonic feeding phase that lasts several weeks before settlement and metamorphosis. Under the same thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] at which the GSI and growth were assessed, the maximum recorded lifespan for Barnea parva is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years], equivalent to about 2190 days. This longevity was inferred from annual growth-ring counts on valves of the largest individuals collected during the population survey and is consistent with the comparatively slow growth and late maturation strategy observed in this species, which appears to trade immediate reproductive output for extended survival across multiple breeding seasons.
